title: To learn to die
hook: Montaigne: to philosophize is to learn to die, and he'd like death to find him planting cabbages

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Lucretius, whose mirror is the time before we were born. Your line was a mirror of the time to come.
screen: `A MIRROR OF THE TIME TO COME.`

segments.voice: A man sits at a writing table in France, working on short pieces that wander from quotation to gossip to confession and back. He is not a priest or a professor. He is a reader who wants to know how to live. One piece takes its title from a line of Cicero's: that to philosophize is to learn to die. Michel de Montaigne writes it plainly, and somewhere in it he says how he would like death to find him. Not in some grand last scene. Planting cabbages.
screen: `A MAN AT A WRITING TABLE.` → `AN OLD ROMAN SAYING.` → `PLANTING CABBAGES.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Montaigne opens by citing Cicero: to philosophize is nothing other than to prepare for death. He takes the line seriously, then makes it his own. Second, the usual remedy, and his complaint. Ordinary people, he says, deal with death by not thinking about it, and he calls that a kind of blindness: when it comes, to them or to someone they love, it lands with full force on someone unprepared. His answer: take away death's strangeness. Spend time with it. Get used to it. Keep it in mind often, not to be gloomy, but so it stops being a stranger at the door. Third, why bother. To think ahead about death, he says, is to think ahead about freedom: a person who has learned how to die has unlearned how to be a slave. Knowing how to die, he goes on, frees us from every kind of subjection and constraint. Loosen that one fear, and much else loosens. Fourth, the cabbages. Here's the turn. He doesn't want to spend his life brooding. He wants to be busy with ordinary work, and he'd like death to find him planting his cabbages, not caring about death, and caring even less about the garden left unfinished. That's the week, too: five answers to suffering kept apart, Socrates's either way, Plato's practice of letting go, Lucretius's mirror, and now Montaigne, learning to die so that he can go on planting.
screen: `TO PHILOSOPHIZE IS TO PREPARE FOR DEATH.` · `TAKE AWAY ITS STRANGENESS.` · `LEARN TO DIE, UNLEARN BEING A SLAVE.` · `FOUND PLANTING CABBAGES.` · then, large: `LEARN TO DIE.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle, and you can skip it; if a loss is close right now, rest in the breath instead. If you'd like, picture once, calmly, the plain fact that a day will come, no accident, no hospital drama, and hold it for a few breaths, the way you'd look at a stranger's face until it looks less strange. Then let it go, and see yourself doing something ordinary that you love: your own cabbages.
Montaigne, who took Cicero's line that to philosophize is to learn to die, and hoped to be found planting his cabbages. Today's word.
Your line: learn to die. Then back to the garden. That's day seven hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne take his essay as an invitation to think about death calmly and often, not to dwell on it, but to loosen the fear and get on with ordinary life.

notes: Montaigne paraphrased throughout (Cotton and Florio are public domain but not on the validator's list).

Check paraphrases: Cicero's opening line; 'the remedy of the vulgar is not to think on it' as blindness; 'let us rid it of its strangeness, frequent it, get used to it'; 'premeditation of death is premeditation of liberty; who has learned to die has unlearned to serve'; 'I want death to find me planting my cabbages, but careless of death, and still more of my unfinished garden'.
'Most people deal with death by not thinking about it' is attributed to Montaigne ('he says'), not asserted by the script.
Week end (757–763) recalled at the close of the teach.
Hook keeps biography minimal (France, a writer, not clergy or a professor); the etymology of essay was cut under the claims rule.

Editor: 'most people' (a sweeping claim, even attributed) now 'ordinary people', after Montaigne's 'the vulgar'; cut the unchecked 'near the middle' and the hook's 'Today:' formula; howItsDone 'often' softened.

Audit: hook called Cicero's line 'an old Roman saying' (Cicero frames it as Socrates' teaching, Tusculan Disputations 1.74); now 'a line of Cicero's'. Removed 'Not praying' in the hook and the 'at his prayers' myth, which set prayer up as a foil (Montaigne was a Catholic and the essay doesn't contrast the two). The 'handle' gloss on fear was the writer's image presented as Montaigne's view; replaced with his own claim that knowing how to die frees us from all subjection and constraint. Note: 1.20 is Villey's numbering; Cotton's translation numbers it 1.19.
